items.prompt: White to move and would like to castle kingside. Find a legal move.

claims.statement: White is in check.
Castling kingside is not legal, because a king in check cannot castle.
Castling queenside is not legal either.
These five moves are all the legal moves.

hints: Before you plan a move, ask whether the king is attacked right now.
Look at the diagonal from b4 to e1.
Only five moves are legal. Castling is not one of them.
items.explain: The bishop on b4 gives check along the diagonal. The claims show castling in either direction is illegal while the king is in check, and that exactly five moves are legal: four king moves and the pawn block on c3.

feedback_by_move.e1g1: Castling kingside is not legal here: the king is in check, and the claims confirm the move is illegal.

items.prompt: White to move. The bishop on c6 attacks the rook on h1. Castle kingside, if the rules allow it.

claims.statement: Castling kingside is legal.
One black piece attacks the h1 rook.
After castling the rook on f1 is not attacked.
The king on g1 is not attacked.

hints: Which squares must be safe for castling: the rook's square, or the squares the king uses?
The king starts on e1, crosses f1 and lands on g1.
The bishop's line ends on h1, and the king never uses that square.
items.explain: The rook may stand on an attacked square when it castles: only the king's start, crossing and landing squares matter. Here none of them is attacked, and after castling the rook on f1 is also safe.

feedback_by_move.h1g1: Moving the rook is legal, but the claims show castling was legal too, and it also takes the rook off the bishop's line.
feedback_by_move.h1h2: Rh2 gets the rook out of the line, but castling was legal as well; an attacked rook does not stop castling.

items.prompt: White's king stepped to f1 and back earlier in this game; the rooks have not moved. White wants the king on g1 as soon as the rules allow. Play the first move.

claims.statement: Kf1 is legal.
The king cannot jump to g1: castling rights were lost when the king first moved.
Castling queenside is also illegal.

hints: Look at where the king and rooks stand, then ask whether anything has moved in the game.
A king that has moved loses the right to castle for the rest of the game, even if it returns.
Castling is gone, so the king walks: one step at a time.
items.explain: The king stepped away and came back, but the right to castle does not come back. The claims show that e1g1 and e1c1 are both illegal here, so the king has to walk and Kf1 is the first step.

feedback_by_move.e1g1: The claims show e1g1 is illegal: once the king has moved, castling is gone for good, even if the king returns to e1.

items.prompt: White to move. The squares between the king and each rook are empty and no right has been lost. Find a castling move.

claims.statement: Castling queenside is legal.
Castling kingside is not legal.
The f1 square, which the king would cross, is attacked once.

hints: Empty squares are necessary but not enough. Which squares does the black rook attack?
The king crosses a square on the way to g1.
Check the f-file.
items.explain: Empty squares between the pieces are not enough: the king may not cross an attacked square. The rook on f8 attacks f1, so castling kingside is illegal, while queenside is legal.

feedback_by_move.e1g1: The claims show e1g1 is illegal: the king would cross f1, and that square is attacked by the rook on f8.

items.prompt: The score says White played Rad1. Play that move.

claims.statement: The a1 rook can move to d1.
The f1 rook can also move to d1.

hints: Both rooks can reach d1, so the destination alone does not identify the move.
The letter after R tells you where the rook started.
Which rook is on the a-file?
items.explain: Two rooks can reach d1, as the claims show, so the record adds the starting file: Rad1 is the rook from the a-file, Rfd1 the one from the f-file.

feedback_by_move.f1d1: Rf1 can also reach d1 (the claims show both moves are legal), but the score says Rad1: the a shows which rook moves.

items.prompt: White to move. Find the best move; no theme is named.

claims.statement: Rc6 is a legal move.
A black knight stands on c6.
Rc6 is the engine's best move at depth 16.
Rc2 is at least three pawns worse than Rc6.

hints: Which black pieces are attacked, and which defend them?
The counting values are a guide. Do they settle this move?
Look at the rook on c1 and the knight on c6.
items.explain: Rc6 takes a knight that the black rook on d6 defends, so the rook can be recaptured. The engine at depth 16 still rates Rc6 as best and rates a quiet rook move such as Rc2 at least three pawns lower. The counting values do not decide the move.

feedback_by_move.c1c2: Rc2 keeps the rook, but the engine at depth 16 rates it at least three pawns below Rc6.

items.prompt: White to move. Black's bishop on e6 can be taken in two ways. Find the best move.

claims.statement: Nxe6 is a legal move.
Rxe6 is a legal move.
Nxe6 is the engine's best move at depth 16.
Rxe6 is at least two and a half pawns worse than Nxe6.

hints: Two white pieces can capture on e6. Which one risks less?
Count what each capture risks, not only what it takes.
Compare the knight with the rook.
items.explain: Both Nxe6 and Rxe6 are legal. Rxe6 would risk a rook for a bishop, which can look active, but the engine at depth 16 rates it at least two and a half pawns below Nxe6, which is its best move.

feedback_by_move.e1e6: Rxe6 looks forceful, but the engine at depth 16 rates it at least two and a half pawns below Nxe6.

items.prompt: White has just played Rc6, a rook for a bishop. Black to move. Find the best reply.

claims.statement: bxc6 is a legal move.
bxc6 is the engine's best move at depth 16.
Even so, White stands at least three pawns better (White's point of view).
Kh7 is at least one pawn worse than bxc6.

hints: Is the rook on c6 really offered, or is it a trap?
Taking is possible. Ask what the d6 pawn does next.
Look at the pawn on d6 and the squares in front of it.
items.explain: Black can take a rook for a bishop, and bxc6 is the engine's best reply. Even so, the engine rates the position at least three pawns for White, because of the pawn on d6. Winning the exchange did not make Black the better side.

feedback_by_move.g8h7: Kh7 declines the rook, but the engine at depth 16 rates it at least one pawn below bxc6.

items.prompt: White to move. Find the strongest move.

claims.statement: Rh7+ is a legal move.
Rh7+ leads to a forced mate in two.
Qh6 is far worse than Rh7+.

hints: Which move changes the material count the most? Is that the right test here?
The black king has few squares; which white pieces can reach them?
Try a forcing move first: look for a check.
items.explain: Rh7+ gives up a rook, five counting points, yet the engine finds a forced mate in two. The point values are a guide to trades when nothing forcing exists; a forced mate overrides them.

feedback_by_move.d2h6: Qh6 keeps all the material, but the engine at depth 16 rates it far below Rh7+.

items.prompt: White to move. Both captures, Bxe8 and Rxd5, will be answered by a recapture. Which one gains material?

claims.statement: A black rook stands on e8.
A black knight stands on d5.
Bxe8 is the engine's best move at depth 16.
Rxd5 is at least three pawns worse than Bxe8.

hints: Each capture is followed by a recapture. Count points, not pieces.
Which piece does each capturing piece take, and which piece is lost?
A bishop taking a rook and a rook taking a knight do not change the score the same way.
items.explain: Each capture is one piece for one piece, but the pieces differ: Bxe8 takes a rook with a bishop, and Rxd5 takes a knight with a rook. The engine at depth 16 rates Bxe8 best and Rxd5 at least three pawns lower.

feedback_by_move.d1d5: Rxd5 is a one-for-one trade by piece count, but it gives a rook for a knight; the engine at depth 16 rates it at least three pawns below Bxe8.

items.prompt: White has castled and Black's bishop on g4 looks at the knight. White to move. Find a good move; one pawn move near the king is among them.

claims.statement: Rc1 and h3 are both within 40 centipawns of the engine's best move at depth 16.
h4 is at least 70 centipawns worse than the best move.

hints: Some pawn moves next to the king are safe, others are not. Which squares does each one loosen?
h3 asks the bishop on g4 a question.
Compare h3 with h4.
items.explain: The pawn move h3 is within 40 centipawns of the engine's best choice at depth 16, so a move next to the castled king is not a weakness in itself. h4 is rated at least 70 centipawns lower, so which pawn move matters.

feedback_by_move.h2h4: h4 also moves a pawn next to the king, but the engine at depth 16 rates it at least 70 centipawns below the best move.

items.prompt: White's pawn needs three moves to queen, Black's needs four. White to move. Find a move that does not lose.

claims.statement: After Kc5 the position is a draw.
After Kd5 the position is a draw.
After Ke5 the position is a draw.
After h6 White loses.
After Kc6 White loses.

hints: Count the moves each pawn needs, then ask which king can reach the other pawn's path.
The shorter count does not help if the other king stops your pawn.
Look at the king moves toward the b-file.
items.explain: White's pawn is a move ahead in the count, but the tablebase shows h6 loses: the black king stops that pawn while the b-pawn runs. The three king moves toward the b-pawn all draw. A shorter count does not decide a race when the king can interfere.

feedback_by_move.h5h6: h6 follows the shorter count, but the tablebase says it loses.
